questions.stem: In a skills drill, for an iron system with internal energy change 127 kJ and entropy change -32 J per K held at constant volume, compute the Helmholtz free energy change at 436 K in kJ.

options.misconception: Added the T delta S term instead of subtracting
Correct application of the principle
Ignored entropy and reported internal energy alone
Did not convert entropy units to kJ

questions.explanation: Helmholtz free energy is defined as A equals U minus T S, so its change at constant temperature is delta U minus T delta S. With entropy in J per K converted to kJ per K, the value at 436 K is 140.95 kJ; its decrease sets the maximum work obtainable at constant volume and temperature.
questions.hint: Delta A = delta U - T delta S.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Maximum Non-Expansion Work principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a skills drill, a brass process at constant temperature and pressure has delta H -94 kJ and delta S 74 J per K at 492 K; find the maximum non-expansion work in kJ.

options.misconception: Correct application of the principle
Used enthalpy change instead of free energy
Used delta G itself instead of its negative
Used the negative of enthalpy instead of free energy

questions.explanation: At constant temperature and pressure the maximum useful non-expansion work equals minus the change in Gibbs free energy. Computing delta G as delta H minus T delta S gives -130.41 kJ, so the maximum non-expansion work is 130.41 kJ; a negative delta G corresponds to positive work available.
questions.hint: Maximum non-PV work = -delta G.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Otto Cycle Efficiency principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a lab practical, with iron cylinder walls, compression ratio 6, and inlet temperature 280 K, an ideal Otto cycle at gamma 1.4 runs; compute its air-standard thermal efficiency as a percentage.

options.misconception: Used a simple one minus reciprocal ratio expression
Used gamma instead of gamma minus one in the exponent
Correct application of the principle
Reported the reciprocal term without subtracting it

questions.explanation: The ideal Otto efficiency is one minus one over the compression ratio raised to gamma minus one. With compression ratio 6 and gamma 1.4 the exponent is 0.4, giving 51.2 percent; raising the compression ratio increases efficiency but is limited by knock in real engines.
questions.hint: Otto efficiency = 1 - 1/r^(gamma - 1).

questions.learningObjective: Apply Brayton Cycle Efficiency principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a calibration run, with aluminum compressor blades, pressure ratio 8, and inlet temperature 283 K, an ideal Brayton cycle at gamma 1.4 runs. Compute its thermal efficiency as a percentage.

options.misconception: Correct application of the principle
Reported the pressure term itself without subtracting
Flipped the sign of the pressure-ratio exponent
Used gamma instead of (gamma minus one) over gamma

questions.explanation: For an ideal Brayton cycle the efficiency depends on the pressure ratio as one minus rp raised to minus (gamma minus one) over gamma. With rp equal to 8 and gamma 1.4 this gives 44.8 percent; higher pressure ratios improve efficiency at the cost of heavier compressors.
questions.hint: Brayton efficiency = 1 - (1/rp)^((gamma-1)/gamma).

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Carnot Cycle Work principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In an instrument check, an aluminum Carnot engine working between 646 K and 301 K absorbs 1035 J per cycle from the hot reservoir. Calculate the work output per cycle in joules.

options.misconception: Computed the heat rejected rather than the work
Correct application of the principle
Reported the full absorbed heat as work
Added the reservoir ratio to the absorbed heat

questions.explanation: A reversible Carnot engine converts a fraction (1 minus Tc over Th) of the absorbed heat into work. With reservoirs at 646 K and 301 K and heat input 1035 J, the work output is 553 J per cycle; the remainder is rejected to the cold reservoir.
questions.hint: Work = Q_in (1 - T_cold/T_hot) for a Carnot cycle.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Compression-Ignition Cycle Efficiency principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a study session, at compression ratio 11 and cutoff ratio 1.74 with gamma 1.4, an ideal compression-ignition cycle with lead pistons runs; compute its air-standard efficiency as a percentage.

options.misconception: Correct application of the principle
Used gamma rather than gamma minus one
Used the Otto cycle formula and ignored the cutoff ratio
Reported only the cutoff correction, not one minus it

questions.explanation: The compression-ignition cycle efficiency equals one minus one over r to the gamma minus one times a cutoff-ratio factor (rho to the gamma minus one) over (gamma times rho minus one). With r 11 and rho 1.74 the efficiency is 56.7 percent; at a cutoff ratio of one it reduces to the Otto result.
questions.hint: Diesel-type efficiency = 1 - [1/r^(gamma-1)] [(rho^gamma - 1)/(gamma(rho - 1))].

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Rankine Cycle Efficiency principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a research run, a steam Rankine plant with lead piping adds 1863 kJ per kg in the boiler and rejects 821 kJ per kg in the condenser; evaluate the cycle thermal efficiency as a percentage.

options.misconception: Inverted the heat-addition-to-rejection ratio
Reported the rejected-heat fraction as efficiency
Correct application of the principle
Divided net work by the condenser rejection

questions.explanation: Thermal efficiency of any power cycle is net work divided by heat input, which for a Rankine plant is (Qin minus Qout) over Qin. Substituting 1863 and 821 kJ per kg gives 55.9 percent; the condenser rejection is a necessary loss, not part of the useful output.
questions.hint: Efficiency = (Q_boiler - Q_condenser) / Q_boiler.
